databases, schemas, grants,
default privileges and extensions.

terraform-postgresql.wrapped_original_text:
Terraform for PostgreSQL
The PostgreSQL provider lets Terraform manage the objects inside a PostgreSQL server: roles, databases, schemas, grants, default privileges and extensions. A community maintainer publishes it under the source address `cyrilgdn/postgresql` ([provider docs](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/cyrilgdn/postgresql/latest/docs)). It replaced HashiCorp's older provider ([README](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/README.md)). The [Terraform map](../terraform.md) explains Terraform itself.

The provider is a SQL client, not an API client. It opens a database connection as an admin role and runs SQL such as `CREATE ROLE` and `GRANT`. Even a refresh queries the system catalogs, so every plan needs a live connection to the server ([A SQL Client](#a-sql-client-a-sql-client)).

The unit is one server and, by default, one database. A cloud provider usually runs the server, for example Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service). Then two providers share the work ([Two Planes, Two Credentials](#two-planes-two-credentials-two-planes-two-credentials)):

- The AWS provider creates the RDS instance, through the AWS API.
- The PostgreSQL provider creates what lives inside the instance, through a database connection.

Inside the server, access follows three rules that shape every plan:

- A grant resource owns the full privilege set of one role on one kind of object in one schema ([A Grant Owns Its Set](#a-grant-owns-its-set-a-grant-owns-its-set)).
- The owner of an object has all privileges on it without any grant ([Owners Need No Grants](#owners-need-no-grants-owners-need-no-grants)).
- Default privileges apply to objects that one named role creates later ([Default Privileges Follow the Creator](#default-privileges-follow-the-creator-default-privileges-follow-the-creator)).

On RDS, the admin role is not a full superuser, which limits what the provider can do ([The RDS Admin Is Not a Superuser](#the-rds-admin-is-not-a-superuser-the-rds-admin-is-not-a-superuser)).

Now compare Snowflake. A Snowflake future grant and a PostgreSQL default privilege both cover objects that do not exist yet. Snowflake keys the rule on a database or schema; PostgreSQL keys it on the role that creates the objects. Default Privileges Follow the Creator compares the two.

The map has four parts. Mental Models explains the ideas above. Reading a PostgreSQL Configuration says what you will see and where to look first. Pitfalls lists the failures that experienced users plan around. Good and Bad Decisions compares the common design choices.

a-sql-client.wrapped_text:
A SQL Client
Each read, create, update and delete of a
resource first opens a connection to the
server ([connect code](https://github.com/cyri
lgdn/terraform-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.
0/postgresql/helpers.go#L14-L36)). The
provider settings say where and how ([provider
settings](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terrafor
m-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/doc
s/index.html.markdown#L141-L188)):

- `host`, `port`, `database`, `username` and
`password`, or the environment variables
`PGHOST`, `PGPORT`, `PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER` and
`PGPASSWORD`.
- `sslmode`, whose default `require` encrypts
the connection but does not check the server
certificate. `verify-full` checks it.
- `superuser`, which must be `false` on RDS.
- `expected_version`. Without it, each new
connection runs `SELECT VERSION()` to detect
the server's features ([config code](https://g
ithub.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-postgres
ql/blob/v1.27.0/postgresql/config.go#L318-L327
)).

So the machine that runs the plan must reach
the server's port 5432, usually inside a
private network, with a valid password.

two-planes-two-credentials.wrapped_text:
Two Planes, Two Credentials
The AWS API and IAM build the RDS instance. A
database connection and a database role build
what is inside it. Each plane needs its own
credentials. A provider setting can use a data
source, so the PostgreSQL provider can read
its host or password from AWS ([provider docs]
(https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provide
r-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/index.h
tml.markdown#L118-L124)). It cannot safely use
an attribute of an instance that the same run
creates. That is why the instance and the
objects inside it usually live in separate
root modules.
two-planes-two-credentials.wrapped_original_text:

a-grant-owns-its-set.wrapped_text:
A Grant Owns Its Set
One `postgresql_grant` covers one combination
of role, database, schema and object type,
such as "role `app`, tables in schema
`public`". On every create and update, it
revokes all privileges of that combination and
then grants its own list, in one transaction
([grant code](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terr
aform-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/postgre
sql/resource_postgresql_grant.go#L194-L204)).
So any other grant on the same combination,
made by hand or by another resource,
disappears at the next update.

`objects = []` means all objects of that type
that exist at apply time. A refresh checks
every one of them, so a table created later
shows as a difference.

So any other grant on the same combination, made by hand or by another resource, disappears at the next update.

`objects = []` means all objects of that type that exist at apply time. A refresh checks every one of them, so a table created later shows as a difference.

owners-need-no-grants.wrapped_text:
Owners Need No Grants
The owner of a table has all privileges on it,
and PostgreSQL's docs say there is no need to
grant privileges to the owner ([GRANT](https:/
/www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-grant.htm
l)). An owner can, however, revoke its own
privileges ([privileges](https://www.postgresq
l.org/docs/current/ddl-priv.html)). So a
`REVOKE` that a grant resource runs against
the owner really removes the owner's rights.

A table's access list shows these rights as
letters. For example, `app=arwdxt/app` means
that role `app` holds these privileges,
granted by `app`:

| Letter | Privilege |
| --- | --- |
| `r` | SELECT |
| `a` | INSERT |
| `w` | UPDATE |
| `d` | DELETE |
| `D` | TRUNCATE |
| `x` | REFERENCES |
| `t` | TRIGGER |

This entry has no `D`, so `app` cannot run
`TRUNCATE` on the table, even if it owns it
([ACL letters](https://www.postgresql.org/docs
/current/ddl-priv.html)).

default-privileges-follow-the-creator.wrapped_text:
Default Privileges Follow the Creator
`postgresql_default_privileges` runs `ALTER
DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE <owner>`. It
applies only to objects that the `owner` role
creates after the rule exists ([resource doc](
https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider
-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/r/postgr
esql_default_privileges.html.markdown#L33)).
PostgreSQL states that new objects are only
affected by the default privileges of the role
that creates them, and that existing objects
do not change ([ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES](http
s://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-alterd
efaultprivileges.html)).

| | PostgreSQL default privileges | Snowflake
future grants |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keyed by | The role that creates the objects
| The database or schema that holds them |
| Existing objects | Unchanged; add a grant on
existing tables | Unchanged; add an `all`
grant |
| When two rules overlap | Schema-level rules
add to the global ones | Schema-level rules
replace database-level ones |

The Snowflake column comes from Snowflake's
[GRANT docs](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql
-reference/sql/grant-privilege); the
[Snowflake map](../snowflake/terraform-snowfla
ke.md#schema-level-future-grants-win-schema-le
vel-future-grants-win) explains its trap.

the-rds-admin-is-not-a-superuser.wrapped_text:
The RDS Admin Is Not a Superuser
On Amazon RDS, the master user is a member of
the role `rds_superuser`, but it is not a real
superuser ([RDS roles](https://docs.aws.amazon
.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Appendix.Postg
reSQL.CommonDBATasks.Roles.rds_superuser.html)
). The provider must know this: set `superuser
= false`. Then some features are off; for
example, the provider cannot read a role's
password back from the database ([provider doc
s](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provi
der-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/index
.html.markdown#L155-L156)). A password changed
outside Terraform then never shows in a plan.

The provider must know this: set `superuser = false`. Then some features are off; for example, the provider cannot read a role's password back from the database ([provider docs](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/index.html.markdown#L155-L156)). A password changed outside Terraform then never shows in a plan.

pg-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read a PostgreSQL configuration in this order:

1. `required_providers` and the Terraform
version. Provider 1.24.0 is "the first version
compatible with Postgresql 16" ([v1.24.0](http
s://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-pos
tgresql/releases/tag/v1.24.0)). The ephemeral
`password_wo` arrived in 1.26.0 ([v1.26.0](htt
ps://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-po
stgresql/releases/tag/v1.26.0)) and needs
Terraform 1.11.
2. The `provider "postgresql"` block, or its
absence. Find where the host, user, password
and `sslmode` come from, and whether
`superuser = false` is set.
3. The pipeline. Find how the runner reaches
port 5432, and which credentials each stage
gets.
4. The environment inputs. Find which role is
the app's user and owner in each environment.
5. `postgresql_role`: the password source,
`ignore_changes`, and `skip_reassign_owned` or
`skip_drop_role`.
6. `postgresql_database`: the owner,
`prevent_destroy`, and the arguments that
force a replacement.
7. `postgresql_grant`: is the grantee also the
owner, is `objects` empty, and do two
resources cover one combination?
8. `postgresql_default_privileges`: is `owner`
the role that creates the tables?

pg-plan-signals.wrapped_text:
Plan Signals
| Line in the plan | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| The plan fails before any diff with `error
detecting capabilities` or a timeout | The
runner cannot reach the server, or the login
fails. |
| `~ privileges` on a table grant with no code
change | New tables appeared; the apply will
run `REVOKE ALL` and grant again. |
| `-` or `-/+` on `postgresql_database` | The
database will be dropped, with its data. |
| `-` on `postgresql_role` | The role's
objects will be reassigned and dropped in the
default database first. |

plan-needs-the-database.wrapped_text:
Plan Needs the Database
When the state holds PostgreSQL resources, the
plan connects to the server. Without a network
path or with a wrong password, it fails before
any diff, and each attempt can wait up to the
180-second `connect_timeout` ([provider settin
gs](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-prov
ider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/postgresql/provid
er.go#L181-L187)). The provider has no
built-in bastion option; a SOCKS5 proxy
through `ALL_PROXY` works ([provider docs](htt
ps://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-po
stgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/index.html.
markdown#L333-L337)). A runner inside the
private network avoids the problem.

The provider has no built-in bastion option; a SOCKS5 proxy through `ALL_PROXY` works ([provider docs](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/index.html.markdown#L333-L337)). A runner inside the private network avoids the problem.

workspace-and-server-disagree.wrapped_text:
Workspace and Server Can Disagree
The workspace chooses the state, but the `PG*`
environment variables choose the server. When
the object names are the same in every
environment, a local run with the wrong
`PGHOST` changes the wrong server, and the
plan looks normal. Set `host` from a data
source of the environment's instance, so the
workspace decides both.

owner-table-grant-drifts.wrapped_text:
Owner Table Grant Drifts
Some configurations grant table privileges to
the role that also owns the tables, while the
app's migrations create new tables after each
apply. New tables have no explicit access
list, so the next refresh shows the privileges
as missing, and the plan shows `~ privileges`
with no code change. The apply then runs
`REVOKE ALL` and grants the listed privileges
again. If the list lacks `TRUNCATE`, the owner
loses `TRUNCATE` on its existing tables
([issue 627](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terra
form-provider-postgresql/issues/627)). Do not
grant table privileges to the owner: it
already has them.
owner-table-grant-drifts.wrapped_original_text:
Owner Table Grant Drifts
Some configurations grant table privileges to the role that also owns the tables, while the app's migrations create new tables after each apply. New tables have no explicit access list, so the next refresh shows the privileges as missing, and the plan shows `~ privileges` with no code change. The apply then runs `REVOKE ALL` and grants the listed privileges again. If the list lacks `TRUNCATE`, the owner loses `TRUNCATE` on its existing tables ([issue 627](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-postgresql/issues/627)). Do not grant table privileges to the owner: it already has them.

default-privileges-miss-objects.wrapped_text:
Default Privileges Miss Objects
A rule for future tables helps only when its
`owner` is the role that really creates the
tables. If migrations run as the app role, but
the rule names the Terraform admin, new tables
get no privileges for the reader, and queries
fail with "permission denied". The plan shows
nothing, because the rule itself is unchanged.
Use one rule for each role that creates
objects, and a grant for the tables that exist
already.

These pitfalls turn a refactor into a
drop.

dropping-a-role-that-owns-objects.wrapped_text:
Dropping a Role That Owns Objects
When a `postgresql_role` leaves the
configuration, the provider runs `REASSIGN
OWNED` and `DROP OWNED` before `DROP ROLE`
([role doc](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraf
orm-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/d
ocs/r/postgresql_role.html.markdown#L14-L22)).
It does this only in the provider's database.
If the role owns objects in another database,
`DROP ROLE` fails. A rename of the role is an
in-place `ALTER ROLE ... RENAME`. A new
resource address without a `moved` block,
however, plans a drop and a create.

It does this only in the provider's database. If the role owns objects in another database, `DROP ROLE` fails. A rename of the role is an in-place `ALTER ROLE ... RENAME`. destroying-a-database-forces-disconnects.wrapped_text:
Destroying a Database Forces Disconnects
A destroy of `postgresql_database` terminates
the open connections and then runs `DROP
DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE)` on PostgreSQL 13
and later ([database code](https://github.com/
cyrilgdn/terraform-provider-postgresql/blob/v1
.27.0/postgresql/resource_postgresql_database.
go#L240-L290)). A drop cannot be undone ([DROP
DATABASE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/curr
ent/sql-dropdatabase.html)). A change of
`template`, `encoding`, `lc_collate` or
`lc_ctype` also replaces the database. Add
`prevent_destroy` to every database with data.

pg-passwords-in-state.wrapped_text:
Passwords in State
All arguments of `postgresql_role`, including
the password, sit in the state in plain text
([role doc](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraf
orm-provider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/d
ocs/r/postgresql_role.html.markdown#L24)). So
does the master password of an RDS instance
that the AWS provider creates. `password_wo`
keeps a role password out of the state ([role 
doc](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-pro
vider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/r/p
ostgresql_role.html.markdown#L27-L29)).

one-login-role-per-app.wrapped_text:
One Login Role per App
Give each app its own login role, and let that
role own the app's database. The predefined
role `pg_database_owner` owns the `public`
schema, so each database owner governs that
schema ([predefined roles](https://www.postgre
sql.org/docs/current/predefined-roles.html)).
Dashboards and other readers then get their
own roles with only `SELECT`. Sharing the RDS
master user between apps and dashboards is
simpler, but one leaked password then opens
every database on the instance.

Sharing the RDS master user between apps and dashboards is simpler, but one leaked password then opens every database on the instance.

separate-migration-and-reader-roles.wrapped_text:
Separate Migration and Reader Roles
The role that runs migrations creates the
tables, so it owns them. A reader role gets a
grant on the tables that exist and a
default-privileges rule `FOR ROLE <migration
role>` for the tables to come. This pair
covers past and future tables, and nothing in
it drifts when migrations add tables.

reach-the-database-privately.wrapped_text:
Reach the Database Privately
A public database endpoint with an allowlist
for the runner's address is quick to set up,
but it exposes the server to the internet. A
runner inside the private network, or a proxy,
keeps port 5432 private. With `sslmode =
"verify-full"`, the provider also checks that
it talks to the right server ([provider settin
gs](https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-prov
ider-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/inde
x.html.markdown#L157-L163)).

close-the-default-doors.wrapped_text:
Close the Default Doors
PostgreSQL grants `CONNECT` and `TEMPORARY` on
every new database to `PUBLIC`, which means
every role ([privileges](https://www.postgresq
l.org/docs/current/ddl-priv.html)). So any
login role on a shared server can connect to
every app's database. The grant resource docs
show how to revoke these defaults ([grant doc]
(https://github.com/cyrilgdn/terraform-provide
r-postgresql/blob/v1.27.0/website/docs/r/postg
resql_grant.html.markdown#L57-L66)).
